newsitem.title: UK: N.Sea crude under pressure, dates kept for op-toll.
newsitem.headline: N.Sea crude under pressure, dates kept for op-toll.

text.p: North Sea crude markets stayed under severe pressure from oversupply and lack of arbitrage outlets on Friday, despite news that British Petroleum kept all five Brent dates from the chains, traders said.
The oversupply originated in the prompt Dated Brent market, which traded at 48 cents below November paper on Friday, but was now infecting Norwegian and other North Sea grades loading in October.
Outright November Brent was about 10 cents down on the day at $21.80 per barrel, and the Oct/Nov spread weakened by about five cents to trade at +44 cents.

Brent continued to suffer from a closed arbitrage window to the U.S., one of the main users of the crude, largely because strong Europe's refining margins kept the Brent/WTI spread narrow, a trader said.
Traders said BP's keeping all five Brent dates was intended to profit from operational tolerance (op-toll) in the system, rather than pointing to a rise in end-user demand for the crude.
"It must be op-toll rather than trading because the cost of keeping Brent is quite high," said a North Sea equity holder.
"I think all those cargoes will be sold on, and there is already plenty of barrels available," said another.
Two end-September Ekofisk cargoes were sold at Dated Brent +2 and flat, illustrating the lack of prompt demand.

By contrast, Mediterranean crude stayed up, thanks to soaring refining margins and thin Russian exports from the Black Sea. Urals was assessed at Dated -80 cents, in line with recent deals, although some sellers saw higher prices.
A U.S. trader-refiner picked up 130,000 tonnes of end-Sept Urals and was considering moving the cargo to the Caribbean.
Another refiner sold half a 120,000-tonne cargo into Italy at Dated -80 cents c+f Augusta, but dealers said unloading at two ports could prove more costly to the seller.
